prompt:
The Supreme Court en banc, in a decision dated August 26, 2026 and released on September 16, unanimously declared that Article II, Section 26 of the Constitution (‘The State shall guarantee equal access to opportunities for public service, and prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law’) requires Congress to enact a law prohibiting political dynasties. It called the provision a ‘constitutional edict’, not a ‘mere aspirational statement’, and abandoned earlier pronouncements that Section 26 is not self-executing. By a majority vote, it granted mandamus, holding that Congress’s failure to pass such a law for 39 years amounts to grave abuse of discretion. It set no deadline, but told Congress to act ‘with utmost urgency’. It left to Congress the definition of ‘political dynasty’ and the scope of the ban, and it denied a separate petition asking COMELEC to disqualify dynastic candidates without a law.

A senator says in a privilege speech: ‘The Court has no business ordering Congress to legislate. Bills against dynasties have been filed in every Congress. Article II is a list of policies, not commands.’
ask: Evaluate the senator’s statement in light of the decision.
core: Presumption that provisions are self-executing (Manila Prince); ‘shall’ is mandatory
Art. II policies are generally not enforceable (Tañada v. Angara; Kilosbayan), but Sec. 26’s ‘shall … prohibit’ is a specific command to Congress, unlike general policy statements
‘As may be defined by law’ leaves the content to Congress (cf. Santiago v. COMELEC on Art. XVII, Sec. 2), so the Court compelled the act, not its content
Expanded judicial power (Art. VIII, Sec. 1): grave abuse by any branch, including inaction; filing bills is not compliance
Senator’s strongest point: mandamus does not lie to compel discretionary legislative acts; enforcement against Congress is doubtful (separation of powers)
model: The senator is partly right but wrong on the main point. Most Article II provisions are declarations of policy that need legislation and create no judicially enforceable rights (Tañada v. Angara). But provisions are presumed self-executing (Manila Prince), and Sec. 26 is not a general policy: it says the State ‘shall … prohibit political dynasties’. ‘Shall’ imposes a duty on the only branch that can perform it. The phrase ‘as may be defined by law’ means Congress chooses the definition and scope, as Art. XVII, Sec. 2 left the initiative’s details to Congress (Santiago v. COMELEC). The Court respected this: it compelled Congress to act but did not write the law, and it refused to let COMELEC disqualify candidates on its own. Filing bills is not enacting a law; 39 years of inaction is the kind of grave abuse that Art. VIII, Sec. 1 lets the Court correct. The senator’s strongest point is that mandamus does not ordinarily lie to compel a discretionary legislative act, and the Court has no means to enforce its order against Congress. The duty is real; its enforcement remains political.
points: Answer first: partly right, mostly wrong
Self-execution: presumption and the ‘shall … prohibit’ text
Art. II general rule acknowledged and distinguished
‘As may be defined by law’: content left to Congress; COMELEC cannot act alone
Grave abuse by inaction (Art. VIII, Sec. 1); bills ≠ compliance
src: Inquirer: SC grants petition urging Congress to pass law vs dynasties
Manila Times: Court orders Congress: legislate dynasty ban
note: Kapatiran Party v. Congress, G.R. Nos. 263934, 272370, 277747 and 279201 (Aug. 26, 2026; Hernando, J.). The facts here come from the Court’s press briefer and news reports; the site has not checked the full decision. Expect Gatmaytan to ask about it.

prompt:
In the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the Senate sitting as an impeachment court ruled 13–1 on September 23, 2026 that ‘all the Members of the Senate’ in Article XI, Section 3(6) (‘No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate’) refers only to senators legally and actually able to take part in the proceedings at the time of the vote. Senators who are detained, suspended, in hiding, medically incapacitated or beyond the Senate’s coercive processes are not counted. If only 20 senator-judges can take part, 14 votes would convict instead of 16.

Three citizens filed petitions in the Supreme Court. One argued that the Senate effectively amended the Constitution by adding a qualification not found in its text; another, that senators who remain in office must be counted even if detained or in hiding. On September 30, the Court unanimously dismissed the petitions on procedural grounds, including lack of standing and prematurity, without ruling on the merits.
ask: (a) Was the Supreme Court correct in dismissing the petitions? (b) Is the impeachment court’s reading of ‘all the Members’ correct?
core: (a) No vote on the verdict yet: no actual injury, not ripe; citizens’ generalized interest; Court avoids interfering mid-trial
(a) Impeachment is not wholly a political question: the Court may enforce constitutional limits (Francisco), so the issue can return after a verdict
(b) Verba legis: ‘all the Members’ is used deliberately in contrast to ‘Members present’; the Constitution distinguishes them
(b) Avelino counted only members within the coercive jurisdiction, but for a quorum (‘a majority of each House’), not ‘all the Members’
(b) The Senate cannot interpret the Constitution to lower its own threshold; interpretation is for the courts (Endencia)
model: (a) Yes. The petitions were premature. No verdict has been rendered, so no one has yet been convicted or acquitted by an allegedly insufficient vote; the injury is speculative (PACU). Citizens suing on a general interest in the Constitution also lacked standing, and a ruling mid-trial would interfere with a proceeding the Constitution gives to the Senate. But the question is not wholly political: where the Constitution sets a limit such as a vote threshold, the Court may enforce it (Francisco), so it can be raised after the vote. (b) The reading is doubtful. Under verba legis, words are given their ordinary meaning, and the Constitution chooses its words: some provisions speak of ‘Members present’, while Art. XI, Sec. 3(6) and Art. VI, Sec. 16(3) require two-thirds of ‘all the Members’. Avelino v. Cuenco excluded a senator abroad, but only in counting a quorum, which the Constitution defines as ‘a majority of each House’, not as a share of ‘all the Members’. A detained or absent senator remains a Member (Jalosjos). By redefining the denominator, the Senate lowered its own threshold. It cannot do by interpretation what only an amendment can (Endencia).
points: (a) Not a political question; can return later (Francisco)
(b) Answer first and verba legis: ‘all the Members’ vs ‘present’
(b) Endencia / no amendment by interpretation; conclusion

Manila Times: SC dismisses challenges to Senate’s impeachment vote-counting rule
note: Impeachment itself (Art. XI) is outside your coverage, but this question tests interpretation, judicial review and quorum, which are within it. Part (b) argues one side; the Senate’s side relies on Avelino’s ‘coercive jurisdiction’ idea and on the practical need to decide.

prompt: Senator Ronald ‘Bato’ dela Rosa had not attended sessions since November 2025, after reports that the International Criminal Court had issued a warrant for his arrest. On May 11, 2026, the ICC confirmed that its judges had unsealed a warrant charging him with the crime against humanity of murder. That day he appeared in the Senate and voted in a leadership change in which Senator Alan Peter Cayetano was elected Senate President, 13–9 with two abstentions. NBI agents tried to serve the warrant inside the Senate premises. On motion of Senator Rodante Marcoleta, with no objection, the Senate placed dela Rosa under ‘protective custody’. Senate President Cayetano said: ‘We will allow an arrest under the condition that it is a Philippine court.’ The NBI said it would not arrest him ‘for the time being’. Dela Rosa left the Senate premises on May 14; Cayetano said ‘what we’re protecting is the sanctity of the Senate, not him.’
ask: Discuss the constitutional issues raised by the Senate’s actions, including any immunity Senator dela Rosa may invoke.
core: Art. VI, Sec. 11: privilege from arrest only for offenses punishable by not more than six years, while in session; murder as a crime against humanity is punishable far more severely, so no privilege
Jalosjos / Trillanes: membership confers no immunity from lawful process for grave offenses; the people’s mandate does not suspend criminal process
The Senate has no constitutional power to grant ‘protective custody’ against executive enforcement; its powers are quorum, attendance, rules and discipline (Sec. 16)
His vote for Senate President was valid while present; Senate President elected by majority of all Members (13 of 24)
His six-month absence: the Senate may compel attendance and discipline (Sec. 16(2)–(3)); legality of executing an ICC warrant is for the courts
model: Dela Rosa has no immunity from this arrest. Art. VI, Sec. 11 protects a senator from arrest only for offenses punishable by not more than six years, and only while Congress is in session. Murder as a crime against humanity is punishable far more severely, so the privilege does not apply. Membership in Congress does not suspend criminal process for grave offenses (Jalosjos; Trillanes v. Pimentel). The Senate’s ‘protective custody’ has no basis in the Constitution. Each House may elect its officers, determine its rules, compel attendance, and discipline its Members (Sec. 16). None of these lets it shield a Member from law enforcement, which belongs to the Executive. The ‘sanctity of the Senate’ may justify rules on how process is served on its premises, not a refusal to allow service at all. Whether an ICC warrant may be executed in the Philippines after the withdrawal from the Rome Statute is a question for the courts, not the Senate. His vote was valid: he was present, and a Senate President needs a majority of all Members (13 of 24). Finally, his six-month absence was a matter the Senate could have addressed by compelling his attendance or disciplining him.
points: Sec. 11 rule and six-year threshold applied
No constitutional basis for ‘protective custody’; Sec. 16 powers listed

prompt:
On September 24, 2026, President Marcos signed Republic Act No. 12326, which moves the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) from November 2, 2026 to the second Monday of November 2028 and fixes the term of barangay and SK officials at five years. Section 5 provides that incumbent officials shall be deemed to have completed one term ‘considering the extension of their terms to two years’. The BSKE had been postponed twice in thirteen months.

Atty. Romulo Macalintal asked the Supreme Court to declare RA 12326 unconstitutional insofar as it postpones the November 2026 polls. He argues that it violates the one-subject, one-title rule; that letting incumbents stay until 2028 is a ‘legislative appointment’, since barangay officials must be elected; and that the repeated postponements amount to ‘endless extensions’. The Office of the Solicitor General answers that the determination of the term of barangay officials is a political question, and that the hold-over is an incidental consequence of Congress’s valid power to fix the term of office.
core: Political question rejected: Congress’s power over election dates and terms is plenary but subject to constitutional limits on suffrage (Macalintal 2023)

Macalintal 2023 guidelines: postponement is the exception; needs important, substantial or compelling reasons (free and safe elections, protecting suffrage, emergency); not election fatigue or divisiveness; intervals not unduly long; narrowly tailored

Fixing a longer term for future officials is within Congress’s power (Art. X, Sec. 8 leaves barangay terms to law); extending incumbents’ terms without an election is the problem (Caguioa: legislative appointment)
Hold-over extends tenure, not term (Macalintal 2023 majority); but Sec. 5’s own words speak of ‘extension of their terms’
One-subject rule: synchronization and terms of BSKE officials are germane; title construed liberally (Giron)
model: The petition should be granted insofar as RA 12326 postpones the November 2026 elections. First, this is not a political question. Congress has plenary power over election dates and the terms of barangay officials, but Macalintal v. COMELEC (2023) holds that the power is limited by the right of suffrage. Postponement is the exception and must be justified by important, substantial or compelling reasons, such as ensuring safe and honest elections or responding to an emergency. Reasons like election fatigue or divisiveness are not enough. The interval must not be unduly long, and the postponement must be narrowly tailored. RA 12326 states no such reason, and a two-year deferral after two earlier postponements is the kind of remote date that Macalintal calls a badge of unreasonableness. Second, Congress may fix a five-year term for officials elected in the future. But Sec. 5 itself speaks of the ‘extension of their terms’; incumbents would serve years beyond the mandate voters gave them, which is a legislative appointment, not a mere hold-over. Third, the one-subject challenge fails: terms and election dates are germane to the title (Giron). The 2026 elections should proceed or be held as soon as practicable.
points: Political question rejected; plenary but limited power
Term-fixing vs term extension / legislative appointment

note: Pending as of October 8, 2026. The model takes the petitioner’s side; the OSG’s side relies on Congress’s plenary power over terms and on hold-over (the 2023 majority said hold-over extends tenure, not term). Either side can score if it applies the 2023 guidelines.

prompt: Two House members, Reps. Edgar Erice and Leila de Lima, asked the Supreme Court to declare unconstitutional the ₱150.9-billion unprogrammed appropriations in the 2026 General Appropriations Act. They argue that the funds give the President ‘blanket authority to spend’, have no clearly identified source of financing, and ‘invert the constitutional architecture of budgeting’; the funds may be used only when revenue collections exceed targets or when grants or foreign loans materialize. The Department of Budget and Management answers that unprogrammed appropriations are standby appropriations released only upon clearly defined fiscal conditions and are ‘not a lump-sum fund nor a blank check’. The Court heard oral arguments in April 2026 on the consolidated petitions, which also cover the 2024 and 2025 budgets, in which Congress added hundreds of billions of pesos to the unprogrammed appropriations proposed by the President.
core: Standing: legislators (impairment of the power of the purse) and taxpayers (disbursement)
Belgica 2019 upheld the 2014 Unprogrammed Fund: lump sums valid if they meet singular correspondence or have sufficient standards
Araullo: unprogrammed funds may be released only upon certification of excess revenue; standby conditions must be real
Sec. 25(1): Congress may not increase the appropriations recommended by the President: additions to unprogrammed appropriations in 2024–2025 above the President’s proposal are suspect
Belgica 2013: no post-enactment discretion for legislators; insertions identified later are pork
model: The Court should uphold unprogrammed appropriations as a device but strike down the congressional increases. On procedure, the legislators have standing because the case concerns Congress’s power of the purse, and taxpayers may question disbursements. On the merits, Belgica (2019) upheld the Unprogrammed Fund: a standby appropriation is valid if each item has a specified purpose (singular correspondence) and its release depends on clear standards. Araullo adds that the condition must be real: unprogrammed funds may be released only when revenue collections actually exceed targets, as certified. So the 2026 items are valid to the extent each specifies its purpose and its trigger. But Art. VI, Sec. 25(1) bars Congress from increasing the appropriations recommended by the President for the operation of the government. Where Congress added items or amounts to unprogrammed appropriations beyond the President’s budget, as in 2024 and 2025, it exceeded that limit. If legislators later identify the projects funded, it also revives the post-enactment role condemned in Belgica (2013). Valid in principle; void as to congressional increases.

prompt: [Adapted for practice.] The proposed 2027 General Appropriations Bill contains this special provision under ‘Unprogrammed Appropriations’: ‘Fund balances of government-owned or controlled corporations exceeding their operating requirements for two years, as determined by the Secretary of Finance, shall be remitted to the National Treasury and shall be used to fund the projects listed herein.’ A health advocacy group recalls that in December 2025, in Pimentel v. House of Representatives, the Supreme Court voided a similar provision of the 2024 GAA (Special Provision 1(d)) and ordered the return of ₱60 billion that PhilHealth had remitted to the Treasury.
core: A GAA cannot amend substantive law; PhilHealth’s reserve fund is fixed by the UHC Act (Sec. 11) and earmarked sin-tax revenues (Pimentel v. House, 2025)
Sec. 25(2): a provision that changes other laws relates to no particular appropriation: inappropriate provision / rider (Philconsa; Caguioa concurrence in Pimentel)
Sec. 29(3): taxes levied for a special purpose form a special fund and go to that purpose only
Delegating to the Finance Secretary the determination of ‘excess’ funds: only the President may augment, and only from savings within the Executive (Sec. 25(5); Pimentel)
Valid only for GOCCs whose charters allow remittance; void as to funds earmarked by law
model: The provision is void at least as to PhilHealth and any GOCC whose funds are earmarked by law. In Pimentel v. House of Representatives (2025), the Court held that Congress cannot amend substantive laws, such as the Universal Health Care Act’s requirement that PhilHealth keep a reserve fund, through the GAA. A provision that sweeps funds a law reserves for a purpose does not relate to any particular appropriation in the budget; it is an inappropriate provision under Art. VI, Sec. 25(2) (Philconsa v. Enriquez) and could be vetoed separately. Where the funds come from taxes levied for a special purpose, such as earmarked sin taxes, Sec. 29(3) requires them to be treated as a special fund used only for that purpose. The provision also lets the Finance Secretary decide what is ‘excess’ and redirect it to unrelated projects, which is in substance a transfer of appropriations. Only the President may augment, and only from savings within the Executive (Sec. 25(5); Pimentel). As to GOCCs whose charters allow remittance of surplus to the Treasury, the provision may stand, but its use must still follow the GAA.
points: Pimentel holding: GAA cannot amend substantive law
Transfer/augmentation and the Finance Secretary; qualification

prompt:
[Adapted for practice.] After the Supreme Court’s anti-dynasty ruling, Congress passes a law with these provisions, drawn from Senate Bill No. 1901 and House Bill No. 8389:

Sec. 3. Definition. — A political dynasty exists when a spouse or relative within the second degree of consanguinity or affinity of an incumbent elective official holds or runs for an elective office in the same province or city, or for a national elective office, while the incumbent is in office.
Sec. 4. Prohibition. — No person covered by Sec. 3 shall be qualified to run for, or be nominated as a party-list representative for, any elective office.
Sec. 5. No spouse or relative within the second degree of an incumbent shall immediately succeed to the same office.

A congressman whose daughter plans to run for the Senate in 2028 challenges the law. He argues that Congress cannot add qualifications to the offices of Senator and Representative, that the law violates equal protection, and that it unduly restricts the voters’ choice.
core: General rule: Congress cannot add to qualifications the Constitution fixes (SJS v. DDB)
Exception: Art. II, Sec. 26 itself authorizes Congress to ‘prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law’; the disqualification has a constitutional source (Kapatiran 2026)
Equal protection: classification by family relationship is based on substantial distinctions germane to the purpose (equal access; preventing concentration of power)
Second-degree limit and immediate-succession ban are policy choices within ‘as may be defined by law’
Standing: the father suffers no direct injury; the daughter, once a would-be candidate, does
model: The law is valid. On standing, the congressman suffers no direct injury from a disqualification that falls on his daughter; she, as a would-be candidate, is the proper party. On the merits, the general rule is that Congress cannot add to the qualifications the Constitution fixes for Senators and Representatives (SJS v. Dangerous Drugs Board). But that rule protects the Constitution’s own choices, and here the Constitution itself chose otherwise. Art. II, Sec. 26 directs the State to ‘prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law’, and the Supreme Court has held that this is a mandatory command to Congress (Kapatiran Party v. Congress, 2026). A disqualification based on a statutory definition of dynasty therefore rests on a constitutional grant, not on Congress’s unaided power. The classification also satisfies equal protection. Relatives of incumbents form a real class with access to the incumbent’s machinery and resources; the distinction is germane to Sec. 26’s purpose of equal access to public service and applies to all members of the class (cf. Albano). The second-degree limit and the ban on immediate succession are choices Sec. 26 leaves to Congress. The challenge fails.
points: Sec. 26 as constitutional basis for the disqualification (Kapatiran)
Degree and succession rules within ‘as may be defined by law’
